About Views

Bird's-eye-view fusion

LiDAR points in the ego frame, each coloured by the camera that sees it, with nuScenes' annotated boxes overlaid, shown as a scatter, a multi-channel raster (colour, height, intensity), and in 3D. Everything shown here comes from code checked in the BEV fusion checks; how it was built is in the build log.

Sweeps, keyframes and coordinate frames

Each sample is a keyframe partway through its scene, so the Sweeps menu can also show it merged with the LiDAR sweeps captured in the half second before it, which fills in far more of the ground (multisweep checks).

  • Sweep: one full turn of the roof LiDAR (LIDAR_TOP). It spins at 20 Hz in the nuScenes setup, so each sweep is about 50 ms of points. Every sweep is recorded.
  • Keyframe: a sweep that nuScenes also chose as a sample, about every tenth sweep. The table below compares the two.
  • Reference keyframe: the keyframe picked in the Sample menu, the one this page is about. Its boxes are the ones drawn, its ego frame is the one every view uses, and in Multisweep it is the newest sweep in the window, the one the earlier sweeps are lined up to.
  • Ego frame: coordinates attached to the car: origin at the rear axle, x forward, y left, z up. The car moves between sweeps, so each sweep has its own ego frame, wherever the car was at that sweep's timestamp. Every view on this page is drawn in the reference keyframe's ego frame, the one at its timestamp.
  • Global frame: coordinates fixed to the map. nuScenes records the car's pose (position and heading) in it for every sweep and camera image, which is what lets points move between ego frames taken at different times.

How the BEV is built

One sweep

The Reference Keyframe setting: the reference keyframe's sweep on its own.

  1. Read the sweep. Each point comes with x, y, z and intensity, in the LiDAR's own frame.
  2. LiDAR to ego to global. The LiDAR's mounting position and rotation on the car move the points into the ego frame. The car's pose at the sweep's timestamp then moves them into the global frame.
  3. Global to each camera. For each camera, the points go from the global frame into that camera's ego frame, using the car's pose at the image's timestamp, then into the camera's own frame using its mounting. Points behind the camera are dropped.
  4. Camera to pixels. The camera's intrinsic matrix projects each remaining point onto the image: pixel = K · (x, y, z) / z, where z is depth. Points that land outside the image are dropped, and the rest take the image's colour at that pixel, interpolated between neighbouring pixels.
  5. Pick a colour. The cameras are tried in a fixed order and each point keeps the first colour it gets. A point no camera sees stays uncoloured (blue on the charts). There is no occlusion test, so a point hidden from a camera by something nearer takes that nearer object's colour.
  6. Top-down view. The coloured points, in the reference keyframe's ego frame, are plotted by x and y (scatter), or binned into a square grid (raster). In each cell the raster keeps the point nearest the sensor and records its colour, height (z) and intensity. Points tied for nearest are averaged.

Multisweep

  1. Gather the window. The reference keyframe's sweep plus the sweeps just before it. For each sweep, every camera's image nearest in time is picked, if one is within the maximum time gap; otherwise that camera is skipped for that sweep.
  2. Colour each sweep on its own. Steps 1 to 5 above run once per sweep, with that sweep's own car pose and its own matched images, so each sweep is coloured by images from nearly the same moment.
  3. Global to the reference keyframe's ego frame. Each sweep's points, already in the global frame, are moved into the reference keyframe's ego frame with the inverse of the car's pose at the reference keyframe. Anything that stood still lines up across sweeps; anything that moved leaves a trail.
  4. One raster per sweep. Each sweep is binned on the same grid as above. "Nearest the sensor" is measured from that sweep's own ego origin, where the LiDAR actually was when it took the point, not from the reference keyframe's.
  5. Merge, newest first. Each cell takes every channel (colour, height, intensity) from the newest sweep with a point in it. A cell no sweep reached stays empty.

BEV: lidar + camera fusion

Reading the chart

  • Points: each LiDAR point takes the colour of the camera that sees it (bev/fusion.py), then is either plotted directly (scatter) or binned into a fixed-size grid (raster, bev/raster.py, checked by check_raster.py).
  • Blue: LiDAR returns no camera saw. White: cells with no LiDAR return at all.
  • Boxes: annotated box footprints (bev/sample.py), each in its category's colour, per the legend.

The Sweeps menu

  • Reference Keyframe: the reference keyframe's own LiDAR sweep, with nothing added.
  • Multisweep: adds the sweeps just before it. Each is coloured by the camera frames nearest to it in time and moved into the reference keyframe's ego frame, then all are merged on the same grid, each cell keeping the newest sweep that reached it (bev/multisweep.py, checked in the multisweep checks).
  • Trails: boxes are the reference keyframe's, so anything that moved during the window leaves a trail behind its box.
  • Blue bands: the newest sweep to reach those cells had no camera frame close enough in time for that direction. The merge keeps that sweep's uncoloured point rather than an older, coloured one.
  • Views: raster views only, plus source sweep age: how long before the reference keyframe each cell's data was captured.
     

What each view shows

All views are in the reference keyframe's ego frame. The 2D ones are top-down, the car at the origin facing up the chart, within 25 m of it on each side.

  • Raster (color): the points binned into a grid of 0.25 m cells. Each cell shows the camera colour of the point nearest the sensor that landed in it, so it reads like a top-down photo. Blue cells had LiDAR returns but no camera view; white cells had no return. Box footprints are drawn on top.
  • Scatter (color): every LiDAR point plotted on its own, with the same camera colours and boxes. Nothing is merged into cells, so it shows the true point density: dense near the car, sparse rings further out.
  • Raster (height): the same grid, coloured by the height in metres of each cell's nearest point, measured from the ego frame's origin near road level. The road is flat and dark; cars, walls and vegetation stand out brighter.
  • Raster (intensity): the same grid, coloured by how strongly the surface reflected the laser. Lane paint, signs and number plates are typically bright, asphalt dark. The scale stops short of the few brightest cells so they don't flatten the rest.
  • Scatter 3D (color) and Scatter 3D (intensity): every point at its real height, with camera colour or intensity; drag to rotate. Boxes aren't drawn here, because they are flat footprints. Single sweep only: the 3D views plot every point, and a multisweep window has about 10 times as many, which would make each sample's download several times larger and the 3D view slow to rotate. The rasters stay the same size however many sweeps feed them, so multisweep offers rasters only.
  • Raster (source sweep age): multisweep only. How many milliseconds before the reference keyframe each cell's point was captured: the reference keyframe's own sweep is 0, older sweeps are larger. It shows which gaps in the reference keyframe's sweep the older sweeps filled.

Box colours

The 6 most frequent categories across these samples, counted each time the page is built, get their own colour:

  • Car (vehicle.car)
  • Adult pedestrian (human.pedestrian.adult)
  • Barrier (movable_object.barrier)
  • Traffic cone (movable_object.trafficcone)
  • Bicycle (vehicle.bicycle)
  • Construction worker (human.pedestrian.construction_worker)

The colours were checked to stay distinguishable from each other and from the blue "no camera coverage", including for colour-blind viewers. More colours failed that check, so every other category is drawn in near-black, though each still gets its own legend entry.
